title: Assumption Mapping and Testing
intro: Test the belief that would sink the idea, with the cheapest test that could prove it wrong.

learn.title: Find the assumptions
learn.text:
Story-map the idea as if it already existed: each step the customer takes, and under it **what must be true.**

Write each as **“We believe that…”**

try.q: Why write assumptions as “We believe that…”?
options: It keeps the team open to being wrong
It makes every assumption easier to measure later
try.explain: A belief invites a test; a statement invites a defence.

learn.title: Five types
learn.text:
**Desirability:** do they want it?
**Usability:** can they use it?
**Feasibility:** can we build it?
**Viability:** does it work for the business?
**Ethics:** could it harm anyone?

try.q: “Reminders won’t pressure people who said no.” Which type?
try.explain: It asks whether the idea could cause harm.

learn.title: Importance × evidence
learn.text:
Place each assumption on two questions:
**If it’s wrong, does the idea fail?**
**Do we have observed evidence?**

Test the **important, unevidenced** corner first.

try.q: Which assumption do you test first?
try.explain: If it’s wrong, the idea fails and you wouldn’t know.

learn.title: Evidence strength
learn.text:
**Weaker:** what people say (interviews, surveys).
**Stronger:** what people do (prototype tests, fake doors, A/B tests).
**Strongest:** what they give up (effortful sign-ups, pre-orders).

Start cheap, then move up as the signal improves.

try.explain: Giving something up is the clearest signal.

learn.title: Run it well
learn.text:
**Change one thing at a time.**
**Write the pass line before the test.**
**Define who you test with.**

A badly built A/B test is weak evidence; a well-run interview can be strong.

try.q: When should the pass line be written?
options: When the test is half done
try.explain: Otherwise the result can be argued either way.

test.q: How long does story-mapping assumptions take?
options: Around two hours for every step in the map
test.explain: Cheap enough to do for every idea.

test.q: “Admins want colleagues to join in week one.” Which type?
test.explain: It’s about whether they want it.

test.q: What counts as evidence on the evidence axis?
Why start with cheap, weaker tests?
options: They kill bad ideas before costly tests
Stakeholders always prefer the cheapest test available
test.explain: Move to stronger tests as the signal improves.

test.q: Why change only one thing per test?
options: Participants find tests with one change easier to follow
test.explain: You can’t tell which change caused the result.

test.q: Which free book lists evaluative experiments?
test.explain: It’s Creative Commons and lists when to use each experiment.
